title: SpaceX's Record IPO Let a 14-Year Employee Fund a Year of Dreams
excerpt: After SpaceX's June 12 debut minted new millionaires, Brian Aggrey and Phoebe Novack quit their jobs and set a $25,000-a-month budget for 365 days of chasing everything from acting school to sculpture — an experiment they call their "Year of Freak."
body:
• Brian Aggrey, 35, spent 14 years at SpaceX — starting as a 21-year-old intern — and his wife Phoebe Novack, 35, was a senior category manager at Impossible Foods. Both quit their jobs after the IPO.
  • The couple has budgeted $25,000 a month for a full year, through a firm end date of July 31, 2027, calling the experiment their "Year of Freak."
  • SpaceX's June 12 debut was the largest IPO in history, raising $75 billion; shares priced at $135 and closed at about $160, valuing the company near $2.1 trillion and making Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.
  • Their itinerary spans Milan, the Côte d'Azur, Chamonix, Venice, and a fall project in Mexico City tackling the city's water shortages.

Brian Aggrey started at SpaceX as an intern at 21 and stayed for 14 years, rising to senior software engineer on Falcon 9 structures and spacecraft avionics. This summer, he quit. So did his wife, Phoebe Novack, a senior category manager at Impossible Foods. Then they left the country.

The couple is in the middle of what they call their "Year of Freak" — a $25,000-a-month, 365-day sprint through their "biggest, craziest, weirdest dreams," as Novack, 35, put it. July brought Milan and the Côte d'Azur; August meant acting classes for Novack at Fontainebleau's acting school while Aggrey biked nearby forests on a used Peugeot and slipped to Valencia to photograph a total solar eclipse; September brought paragliding in Chamonix, the Italian Grand Prix and the Venice Biennale. Next: Mexico City this fall, where Aggrey will study sculpture and collaborate on a project addressing the city's water shortages — then back to California for an El Niño winter. The experiment ends, by design, on July 31, 2027.

Fourteen years of stock options, and one lucky bet

Aggrey, 35, joined SpaceX a decade after it was incorporated and had wanted to work on rockets since middle school. Over his tenure he built a sizable stake from his signing allocation and annual performance bonuses — money that felt theoretical for years. The couple met at Washington University in St. Louis; in leaner times, Aggrey once needed a roommate to front him $200.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=UzLfTTwFN0U

"We're in this position because of how well SpaceX stock did. We had no idea, while we were going through it, accumulating stock, whether it was ever going to be worth anything."

— Brian Aggrey, former SpaceX senior software engineer

The biggest IPO in history

SpaceX's June 12 debut was the largest IPO in history: 555.6 million shares priced at $135, raising $75 billion — dwarfing Saudi Aramco's $25.6 billion 2019 debut. Shares closed near $160, valuing the company at roughly $2.1 trillion and making Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire, per market coverage of the listing.

The windfall landed across the workforce, not just at the top; some of Aggrey and Novack's peers are weighing retirement and new homes, the couple said. To fund their year, they sold enough shares to feel insulated from volatility but kept most of their stake. "The IPO really gave us the confidence to treat that stake as real capital," Aggrey said. "We're privileged to be in this place. It's been a long road."

Acting classes, sculpture and a water crisis

Novack's summer at Fonact, the Fontainebleau School of Acting, meant 35-hour weeks with students aged 16 to 72, ending in a Chekhov showcase. Of the Valencia eclipse, Aggrey said: "The sun's corona, its atmosphere, is always there. But I could only see it, and all its colors, when the sun was blocked out. It was a great allegory for this year itself."

The Mexico City leg is the year's most ambitious creative project: Aggrey will collaborate with sculptor Brian Thoreen, who works in bronze, leather and earthen materials, on work aimed at new solutions to the city's water shortages. Novack plans classes in landscape design, visual arts and film production. "I've spent 13 years being like, 'No, I can't do that,'" she said. "Now it is: 'No, we do everything, and there's no limit — for one year.'"

The diaspora angle

The couple has no stated Indian connection, but the story echoes a playbook familiar to Indian engineers in Silicon Valley: years of grinding at a private company, options nobody can price, and one liquidity event that changes everything.

What happens after July 2027

The July 31, 2027 deadline is deliberate. After that, they may return to careers like the ones they left or pivot — Aggrey is newly interested in improving U.S. infrastructure systems.

"I think it is going to be very important for the second half of our lives to have had this experience and been like 'Yeah, OK, we tried things differently.'"

— Brian Aggrey, former SpaceX senior software engineer
